By means of model dependent analyses based on spatial and spectral templates, a purely diffuse neutrino flux was measured in which no individual source was resolved. We present here a novel theoretical computation about the expected neutrino emission from the Galactic Plane that, differently from previous models, includes both the contributions from cosmic-ray (CR) sea and hadronic sources, represented by star clusters and supernova remnants therein, which are to date believed to be the dominant sources of Galactic CR protons. For the modelling of sources, diffusive particle acceleration is considered at both the collective wind termination shock blown by member stars and at the supernova shocks. The predicted flux of very-high energy neutrinos from individual star clusters is found to be marginally detectable even by cubic kilometer scale detectors, such that their cumulative contribution is expected to appear as an unresolved diffuse component, on top of that guaranteed by the CR sea interacting with the gas along the Plane. The overall neutrino production of the Milky Way star cluster population is computed, based on multiple synthetic realizations of the cluster population reproducing local stellar observations. As a result, we obtain novel neutrino template maps and provide them to the community, to be tested in future neutrino analyses in order to constrain the role of star clusters for extreme CR acceleration and neutrino production. The normalization of our models is consistent with the IceCube best-fit of existing Galactic templates, suggesting that the unresolved contribution from cluster emission may be non-negligible.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a new model including star clusters and supernova remnants as Galactic neutrino sources, predicting a marginally detectable neutrino flux that may explain part of the diffuse neutrino background observed by IceCube, supported by synthetic cluster population simulations and template maps for future testing.
AI.motivation: To improve the theoretical modeling of Galactic neutrino emission by including contributions from both cosmic-ray sea and hadronic sources within the Galactic Plane, particularly focusing on star clusters and supernova remnants as dominant sources of Galactic cosmic-ray protons.
AI.method: Developed a novel theoretical computation incorporating particle acceleration at stellar wind termination shocks and supernova shocks within star clusters. Multiple synthetic realizations of the cluster population were generated based on local stellar observations to predict neutrino flux and produce neutrino template maps for the Galactic Plane.
AI.result: The cumulative neutrino flux from individual star clusters is marginally detectable by current large-scale neutrino detectors, contributing as an unresolved diffuse component in addition to that from the cosmic-ray sea. The model's normalization aligns with IceCube's best-fit Galactic templates, indicating that star cluster emission may play a significant role in neutrino production.
AI.conclusion: The unresolved neutrino emission from star clusters within the Milky Way likely contributes non-negligibly to the diffuse Galactic neutrino flux detected by IceCube. The presented neutrino template maps serve as a valuable tool for future analyses to further constrain the role of star clusters in cosmic-ray acceleration and neutrino production.

title: Universal Suppression of Gravitational Waves from Black Hole Evaporation Dynamics
comment: 5-page Letter + Supplemental Material (12 pages total); 2 figures
summary: Evaporating black holes can leave distinct imprints on gravitational wave (GW) backgrounds. We show that black hole populations with finite width mass distributions exhibit a universal late time evolution governed by the evaporation dynamics rather than the details of the initial mass distribution, leading to a characteristic power law suppression of the induced GWs. We demonstrate this for a broad class of mass functions in primordial black hole (PBH) scenarios featuring an early Universe matter-dominated era, and identify the suppression of PBH-induced GWs found for critical collapse distributions as a manifestation of this general phenomenon. Our results establish a direct connection between the asymptotic GW spectrum and the underlying law of black hole evaporation.

AI.tldr: Evaporating primordial black holes imprint a universal power law suppression on gravitational wave backgrounds at late times, governed by evaporation physics rather than initial mass distributions, revealing a direct link between GW signals and black hole evaporation laws.
AI.motivation: To understand how evaporating black holes impact gravitational wave backgrounds and whether the GW signals reflect the underlying evaporation dynamics rather than initial mass distributions.
AI.method: Analyze the evolution of gravitational wave backgrounds generated by black hole populations with finite-width mass distributions, focusing on primordial black holes during an early matter-dominated era, and compare the resulting GW spectra across different mass functions.
AI.result: Identification of a universal late-time evolution of GW backgrounds governed by black hole evaporation dynamics, leading to a characteristic power law suppression of induced GWs regardless of initial mass distribution details; demonstrated explicitly for various mass functions and linked to previously observed GW suppression in critical collapse scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The asymptotic gravitational wave spectrum directly encodes the fundamental black hole evaporation law, providing a universal signature that transcends specific initial mass distributions in primordial black hole populations.

title: Measuring the radii of merging neutron stars with asteroseismology
comment: Main text and Methods: 19 pages. 29 pages including extended data and supplementary material. Submitted
summary: The structure and dynamics of neutron stars can be used to probe the physics of extreme matter at nuclear densities and beyond. Nucleonic matter up to ~2-3 times nuclear saturation density is well-studied by nuclear experiments and theoretical modelling. Matter beyond these densities may contain non-nucleonic degrees of freedom that determine the structure of the neutron star inner core and influence bulk observables like stellar radius. Neutron star radius is a key parameter for constraining the core equation of state, but is not a direct gravitational-wave observable during neutron star mergers. Here we show that, if nucleonic physics is well constrained at low densities, the frequency of the asteroseismic crust-core interface mode in a neutron star can be used to infer its radius to within 5-10%, in a way which is notably insensitive to the details of the inner core. This frequency can be measured through multimessenger coincident timing of resonant shattering flares, or direct observation of dynamical tidal resonance with next-generation gravitational-wave detectors. We show that improved constraints on low-density nucleonic physics by nuclear experimental and theoretical efforts will substantially improve such a radius measurement, leveraging low-density efforts for an improved understanding of physics at higher densities.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that the neutron star radius can be accurately measured using the frequency of crust-core interface asteroseismic modes, provided low-density nucleonic physics is well-constrained, thus improving understanding of dense matter physics in neutron stars.
AI.motivation: To understand the physics of extreme matter in neutron stars by characterizing their structure and dynamics, especially beyond nuclear saturation density where non-nucleonic matter may appear.
AI.method: Use the frequency of the asteroseismic crust-core interface mode, measurable via multimessenger observations like resonant shattering flares or dynamical tidal resonances in gravitational-wave detectors, combined with well-constrained low-density nucleonic physics.
AI.result: The neutron star radius can be inferred with 5-10% accuracy, largely independent of inner core details, enabling better constraints on the equation of state of dense matter.
AI.conclusion: Constraining low-density nucleonic physics improves radius measurements of neutron stars via asteroseismic modes, which provides key insights into the core equation of state and high-density physics beyond current experimental reach.

title: Inflationary interpretation of the gravitational-wave signal in the European Pulsar Timing Array DR2 with constraints
summary: The second data release of the European Pulsar Timing Array (EPTA) collaboration provides evidence for the presence of a gravitational-wave (GW) background. In this work, we explore a potential cosmological interpretation of this signal in terms of inflationary scenarios. We parametrize the tensor power spectrum in terms of the tensor-to-scalar ratio $r$, the tensor spectral index $n_t$, the reheating temperature $T_{\text{rh}}$, and the cut-off frequency $f_{\text{end}}$. We incorporate all relevant observational constraints, including those from the Cosmic Microwave Background, Big Bang Nucleosynthesis, and LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA observations. We demonstrate that imposing these constraints consistently reduces the region of parameter space that provides a viable interpretation of the EPTA signal, to $-11.66 \lesssim \log_{10}r \lesssim -1.45$, $1.32 \lesssim n_t \lesssim 2.47$, $1.78\text{ MeV} \lesssim T_{\text{rh}} \lesssim 28.2\text{ GeV}$, and $75.86\text{ nHz} \lesssim f_{\text{end}} \lesssim 14.45\text{ Hz}$ at the 95% confidence level. This favours the scenario in which the GW spectrum in the EPTA frequency band originates from tensor modes that re-entered the Hubble radius during the radiation-dominated era, allowing for a higher $r$ and a flatter spectrum. However, $T_{\text{rh}}$ must take very low values, which are challenging to explain theoretically.

AI.tldr: The EPTA gravitational-wave background likely originates from inflationary tensor modes constrained by multiple cosmological observations, favoring a low reheating temperature and a flatter tensor spectrum, though the required low reheating temperature poses theoretical challenges.
AI.motivation: To explore a cosmological interpretation of the gravitational-wave background signal detected by the EPTA in terms of inflationary models.
AI.method: Parameterization of the tensor power spectrum using tensor-to-scalar ratio, tensor spectral index, reheating temperature, and cutoff frequency; incorporation of constraints from CMB, BBN, and LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA observations to limit the parameter space.
AI.result: The viable parameter space for interpreting the EPTA signal is constrained to specific ranges for r, n_t, T_rh, and f_end, favoring tensor modes re-entering the horizon during radiation domination with low reheating temperatures that are theoretically challenging.
AI.conclusion: The EPTA gravitational-wave background signal can be explained by inflationary tensor modes re-entering during the radiation era, but requires unusually low reheating temperatures and a flattened tensor spectrum within constrained parameter ranges.
